title: Google to require AI agents to use official connections to Workspace data
excerpt: From 1 February 2027, AI agents must reach Google Workspace email, files and calendars through official agent connections, with new controls for approvals, audit logs and revoking access.

sources.title: Google Workspace Updates: Simplifying agent access while keeping organizations in control
Google Workspace Blog: Built for trust and control: new AI agent protections and developer tools
Superpower Daily: Google sets February deadline for AI agents to switch how they access Workspace
Jazz: Google Workspace MCP requirement for AI agents: what changes

body_html:
Google has told organisations that use its Google Workspace office tools that, from 1 February 2027, AI agents will have to reach Workspace data through official agent connections rather than by calling Workspace's programming interfaces directly. Google announced the change in posts on 24 and 25 November 2026, alongside new controls that let companies and schools see, limit and switch off AI agents that work with their email, files and calendars. The change applies worldwide.

What changes

An AI agent is software that can take actions for a person, such as reading email, filing documents or booking meetings. Until now, agents could connect to Workspace in the same way as any other app. Google says agents must instead use its Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace command-line tool, both now generally available. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data.

Google's Workspace Updates blog says "technical enforcement begins" on 1 February 2027. Google's posts do not spell out what happens to agents that still connect the old way. Secondary reports differ: one says the old route closes, while a security vendor reading Google's developer guides says such traffic would be limited rather than refused. This is not yet clear.

Google also introduced usage tiers. It says over 99% of active developers fall in a free Standard tier, and charges for heavy use under a Scaled tier start on 1 April 2027.

The controls Google describes

In a post by Yulie Kwon Kim, Workspace's vice president of product, Google lists six protections. In short:

  • Checks on every request: each agent request is checked against the user's permissions, the organisation's data loss prevention rules and its labels for sensitive files.
  • Clear identity: outside agents must identify themselves with their own credentials and ask only for the access they need. Time-limited approvals are "coming soon".
  • Human confirmation: organisations can require a person to approve high-impact actions, such as sending email outside the organisation, changing sharing on files or making bulk edits.
  • Visibility and a way to stop: administrators get agent activity logs and can revoke an agent's access. Google says users will be able to see and revoke agents themselves later.
  • Restricted areas: a coming feature would block outside agents from email messages and chosen files or folders.
  • Limits on data use: a new contract addendum for agent makers bars them from keeping raw data permanently, training models on it or scraping it, and requires deletion when a user disconnects.

Google explains the reason plainly: agents can "take unintended actions" and move or change data "at machine speed". Its post states the principle as "your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it."

What is still unknown

Several features are announced as coming later, with no dates. It is not yet clear how strictly the 1 February rule will be applied to existing tools, or which Workspace editions get every audit feature. Prompt injection, where hidden instructions in a document or email try to steer an agent, is not addressed directly in the posts.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

When AI agents work inside the systems that hold people's email and files, the key questions are who let the agent in, what it may do, and how to stop it. Requiring agents to identify themselves and use a checked entrance supports D2 Bounded autonomy and D6 Secure and supported. Human approval for risky actions and the ability to revoke access support D1 Always stoppable. Logs of agent activity support D9 Accountable, and limits on keeping and training on data support D5 Private by default.

Organisations using any office platform can ask the same questions of every agent they connect; Humasure's security page and questions to ask any maker are a starting point.
